text: Definition 2.1 (Frontier) . A frontier $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\}$ is a complete cut of the tree, meaning that every root-to-leaf path intersects $\mathcal{F}$ in exactly one node.

Definition 2.2 (Fast oracle $F$ ) . The fast oracle returns a deterministic value $V_{F}(v)$ . Equivalently, $\nu_{v,1}$ is a degenerate distribution at $V_{F}(v)$ , so $\mu_{v,1}=V_{F}(v)$ and $|V_{F}(v)-V^{*}(v)|\leq B(h(v)).$

Definition 2.3 (Slow oracle $S$ ) . For each node $v$ , repeated slow-oracle queries return independent $\sigma$ -sub-Gaussian samples $Y_{v,s}$ with distribution $\nu_{v,2}$ and mean $\mu_{v,2}=V^{*}(v).$

Remark 2.1 . The unbiased slow oracle setup is analogous to that of Kaufmann and Koolen [5] , which defines the sampling oracle as mean-correct $\mathbb{E}[Y_{l,s}]=V^{*}(l)$ ; in § 4 , we instantiate it by adding actual noise to true minimax values. Also, unlike classical BAI-MCTS [ 5 ] , where stochastic samples are attached to leaf rollouts, our slow oracle may be queried at any exposed non-root node. In § 3.2 , we add further worst-case guarantee to real-world applications, where slow-oracles are biased.

Remark 2.2 (Fast-oracle envelop) . We note that the envelope structure in Eq. ( 1 ) can be motivated by finite horizon MARL. Specifically, for a critic $\widehat{V}_{t}$ with the correct terminal value, discount $0\leq\gamma\leq 1$ , and minimax Bellman residual $\eta_{t}=\lVert\widehat{V}_{t}-\mathcal{T}_{t}\widehat{V}_{t+1}\rVert_{\infty}$ , Bellman nonexpansiveness gives $\lVert\widehat{V}_{t}-V_{t}^{*}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\sum_{j=t}^{H-1}\gamma^{j-t}\eta_{j}$ . A known bound $\eta_{j}\leq\bar{\eta}$ provides the nondecreasing envelope $B(h)=\bar{\eta}\sum_{i=0}^{h-1}\gamma^{i}$ .

Definition 2.4 (Effective gap) . Set the root effective gap to $\Delta_{r}^{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneqq\Delta_{*}$ . For every non-root node $v$ , let $p(v)$ denotes the parent of $v$ , we define recursively $\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneqq\max\!\left\{\Delta_{p(v)}^{\mathrm{eff}},\,|V^{*}(v)-V^{*}(p(v))|\right\}.$

Remark 2.5 . We note that instance-dependent complexity measures are standard in fixed-confidence BAI. Classical bounds are often stated in terms of gap-dependent hardness quantities such as $H_{1}=\sum_{i\neq i^{*}}\Delta_{i}^{-2}$ , while refined analyses use information-theoretic characteristic times to quantify the intrinsic difficulty of an instance [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] . BAI-MCTS and multi-fidelity BAI follow the same convention, using tree- or fidelity-dependent oracle complexities to state adaptive cost guarantees [ 5 , 2 , 4 ] . Our $H^{*}$ serves as an analysis-only recursive oracle complexity under perfect gap information, rather than an information-theoretic lower bound; see Appendix B.8 .

Theorem 3.1 (PAC correctness) . Fix any feasible confidence allocation $\boldsymbol{\delta}=(\delta_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\}}$ and any $\varepsilon\geq 0$ . Consider Algorithm 1 run with accuracy $\varepsilon$ , let $\tau$ be its stopping time, and, on the event $\{\tau<\infty\}$ , let $\hat{a}_{\tau}$ be the returned root child. Then, $\mathbb{P}\!\left(\tau<\infty\text{ \emph{and} }V^{*}(r,a^{*})-V^{*}(r,\hat{a}_{\tau})>\varepsilon\right)\leq\delta$ . In fact, on the simultaneous-validity event $\mathcal{E}_{\delta}$ , every finite-time recommendation made by the stopping rule is $\varepsilon$ -optimal.

Remark 3.2 . We note that Theorem 3.1 uses only simultaneous interval validity and the root stopping rule and does not use any assumptions in the later upper-bound proof. Its proof is very straightforward, and we defer it to Appendix B.4 . The finite stopping guarantee is elaborated in Theorem 3.6 .

Assumption 3.3 (Local dyadic scale regularity) . Fix the confidence allocation $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ , we assume there exist constants $\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}\geq 1$ and $\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}\geq 1$ such that, for every non-root node $v$ and every $K\geq 0$ , $\sum_{j=0}^{K}\Gamma_{v}^{(j)}(\delta_{v})\leq\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}\Gamma_{v}^{(K)}(\delta_{v}),$ (10) and, for every non-root node $v$ , $\Gamma_{v}\!\left(\frac{\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}}}{2},\delta_{v}\right)\leq\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}\,\Gamma_{v}(\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}},\delta_{v}).$ (11) We write $\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}}\coloneqq\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}$ .

Remark 3.4 . Assumption 3.3 is purely local: it does not compare the raw recursive dyadic DP with $J^{*}$ . The prefix condition is the standard dyadic regularity of a statistical sample-complexity curve; it holds with a constant for polynomial laws, e.g., $m_{v}(\rho,\delta_{v})\asymp\rho^{-2}\log(1/\delta_{v})$ with uniform comparison constants over the positive-cost scales. The second condition only asks that moving from the effective gap to the neighboring dyadic half-scale changes the local stop cost by at most a constant factor. This is the only place where the deterministic fast-bias cutoff in Eq. ( 7 ) can create a knife-edge, which is ruled out by the assumption at the exact effective gap.

Theorem 3.6 (General-depth upper bound) . Fix any feasible confidence allocation $\boldsymbol{\delta}=(\delta_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\}}$ satisfying Assumption 3.3 , and run Algorithm 1 with $\varepsilon=0$ . On $\mathcal{E}_{\delta}$ , the algorithm is guaranteed to stop at a finite time $\tau$ , returns $\hat{a}_{\tau}=a^{*}$ , and satisfies $C_{\tau}\leq P_{D}\,H(\boldsymbol{\delta})$ . With the depth budgets $\alpha_{h}=(h+1)^{2}$ , the cost $C_{\tau}\leq\mathcal{O}_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}\!\left(D^{2}H(\boldsymbol{\delta})\right)$ . Consequently, suppose the regularity constants $\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}$ and $\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}$ are uniform along a near-optimal feasible sequence: for every $\eta>0$ , there exists a feasible allocation $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\eta}$ satisfying Assumption 3.3 with these same constants and $H(\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\eta})\leq H^{*}+\eta.$ Then, the corresponding run satisfies, with probability at least $1-\delta$ , $\hat{a}_{\tau}=a^{*},\qquad C_{\tau}\leq P_{D}\bigl(H^{*}+\eta\bigr).$ In particular, when $\alpha_{h}=(h+1)^{2}$ and the local regularity constants are uniform constants, $C_{\tau}\leq\mathcal{O}_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}\!\left(D^{2}(H^{*}+\eta)\right),$ and, since $H^{*}\geq|\mathrm{Ch}(r)|\geq 2$ , one obtains $\mathcal{O}_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}(D^{2}H^{*})$ by taking $\eta\leq H^{*}$ , or $\eta=0$ whenever the infimum in Eq. ( 9 ) is attained with the same regularity constants.

Theorem 3.7 . Suppose the slow oracle has fixed mean $V^{*}(v)+b_{v}$ , with known $\xi\geq\max_{v}|b_{v}|$ , and its samples satisfy Eq. ( 3 ) around this mean. Replacing each slow radius $\beta_{v}$ by $\beta_{v}+\xi$ preserves the $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ finite-output correctness of 2FFS. The bias inflation does not accumulate with tree depth.

Theorem 3.8 . Let $B(h)$ denote the true fast-oracle envelope, and let $\hat{B}(h)$ be a nondecreasing proxy envelope with $\hat{B}(0)=0$ and $\hat{B}(h)\geq B(h)$ for all $h$ . Replacing $B(h)$ with $\hat{B}(h)$ preserves the finite-output PAC guarantee and, on $\mathcal{E}_{\delta}$ for the same query history, can only widen the resulting confidence intervals.

Remark B.1 (Scale-synchronous progress) . Recursive descent is required to remain synchronized with the current parent obligation and its remaining recursive budget. Concretely, inside a call $\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k,B)$ , a child call $\textsc{Resolve}(u,s^{\prime},K_{s^{\prime}}^{\leq k}(u,t),B_{\mathrm{rec}})$ is admissible only if the scale- $k$ certificate at $v$ is still unresolved at the current round, the child is selected by the current scale- $k$ rule at $v$ , and $B_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is no larger than the remaining budget $\mathsf{B}_{v,k}^{\mathrm{rec}}-M_{v,k}^{\mathrm{exp}}$ . In particular, • in a comparison case, the algorithm may refine only the current blocking contender $b_{s}(v,k,t)\in A_{s}(v,k,t)$ ; the blocker is refined first on $(b_{s}(v,k,t),\bar{s},K_{\bar{s}}^{\leq k}(b_{s}(v,k,t),t))$ whenever this obligation is finite, and otherwise on $(b_{s}(v,k,t),s,K_{s}^{\leq k}(b_{s}(v,k,t),t))$ ; • in a selector case, the algorithm may refine only a child $u\in A_{s}(v,k,t)$ with $\neg\mathsf{Comp}_{s}(u,k,t)$ , and it calls that child at $K_{s}^{\leq k}(u,t)$ . Every invocation of $\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k,B)$ performs at most one positive oracle action, either a slow query or an expansion, at the current node or below it. A local query may follow a zero-cost blocked child return. After each positive action, the algorithm updates the intervals, comparison endpoints, blockers, and active child sets before descending again. Thus the coarser-scale tests that could already certify or exclude a child from the current scale- $k$ obligation are checked before that child is refined further.

Definition B.1 (Side-specific scale safety) . Fix a scale index $k\geq 0$ , a round $t$ , an explored non-root node $v$ , and a side $s\in\{L,U\}$ . We say that $v$ is $(s,k)$ -safe at round $t$ if $\begin{cases}V^{*}(v)-L_{v}(t)\leq\rho_{k}/2,&\text{if }s=L,\\[4.0pt] U_{v}(t)-V^{*}(v)\leq\rho_{k}/2,&\text{if }s=U.\end{cases}$

Proposition B.10 (Active-call localization with explicit depth bound) . Assume $\mathcal{E}_{\delta}$ and $\varepsilon=0$ . Consider any invocation $\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k)$ with finite scale $k$ made by Algorithm 1 during an outer-loop iteration. Let $m$ be the number of recursive edges from the initially selected root child in that outer-loop iteration to $v$ . Then $m\leq D$ and $\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}}\leq C_{\mathrm{act}}(D)\rho_{k},\qquad C_{\mathrm{act}}(D)=2.$ Equivalently, every active finite-scale call satisfies $\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}}\leq 2\rho_{k}.$

Definition B.2 (Aggregate subtree call cost) . For a non-root node $v$ , let $\mathfrak{C}_{v}(t)$ be the sum of the costs returned by all invocations at $v$ in the first $t$ completed outer-loop rounds. Equivalently, this is the slow cost at $v$ , together with all fast and slow costs strictly below $v$ ; it excludes the fast query that first exposed $v$ . Set this quantity to zero for an unexposed node. Write $L_{v}^{\mathrm{cost}}(t)$ for the direct slow cost at $v$ , and $E_{v}^{\mathrm{cost}}(t)$ for the remaining, recursive cost. Then $\mathfrak{C}_{v}(t)=L_{v}^{\mathrm{cost}}(t)+E_{v}^{\mathrm{cost}}(t),\qquad E_{v}^{\mathrm{cost}}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{v\text{ expanded by }t\}|\mathrm{Ch}(v)|+\sum_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}\mathfrak{C}_{u}(t).$ The second term is zero at a leaf. Costs in a child subtree also appear in its ancestors’ costs, but no sum over all nodes is used: the root-child subtrees are disjoint, and their sum counts every post-initialization oracle cost exactly once.

Proposition B.16 (Aggregate subtree charging) . Assume $\mathcal{E}_{\delta}$ , $\varepsilon=0$ , and Assumption 3.3 , and let $P_{h}$ be defined in Eq. ( 12 ). For every finite round $T$ and every non-root node $v$ , $\mathfrak{C}_{v}(T)\leq P_{h(v)}J_{v}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\delta}).$ In fact, for every currently unresolved finite obligation $(v,s,k)$ with $\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}}\leq 2\rho_{k}$ , the stronger bound holds: $\mathfrak{C}_{v}(T)+d_{v}(s,k;T)\leq P_{h(v)}J_{v}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\delta}).$ (13) Consequently, $C_{T}\leq|\mathrm{Ch}(r)|+P_{D-1}\sum_{a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)}J_{a}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\delta})\leq P_{D}H(\boldsymbol{\delta}).$ For $\alpha_{h}=(h+1)^{2}$ , $P_{D}\leq\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}}(1+\alpha_{D})\prod_{i=1}^{D}\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}}{\alpha_{i}}\right),$ so $P_{D}=O_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}(D^{2})$ .

Proposition B.19 (Finite stopping and correctness) . Assume $\mathcal{E}_{\delta}$ , $\varepsilon=0$ , and Assumption 3.3 . Then Algorithm 1 halts after finitely many oracle calls. At its stopping time $\tau$ , every returned action $\hat{a}_{\tau}$ is the unique optimal root action $a^{*}$ .
